{
  "schema": "threatline.threatmodel.v1",
  "issueKey": "EVAL-02",
  "sketch": {
    "components": ["SFTP server", "Partner file drop directory", "CSV parser job", "Orders import pipeline"],
    "dataStores": ["Orders database", "SFTP file storage"],
    "externalServices": ["Partner systems (SFTP clients)"],
    "trustBoundaries": ["Partner -> SFTP server", "SFTP storage -> parser job", "Parser job -> orders database"],
    "dataClasses": ["pii"],
    "exposure": "partner",
    "llmFeatures": false
  },
  "threats": [
    {
      "stride": "Tampering",
      "title": "Malicious CSV content injected straight into the orders database",
      "scenario": "A partner (or anyone who obtains partner SFTP access) uploads a CSV whose fields contain SQL fragments, oversized values or extra columns. If the parser builds SQL by concatenating row values instead of using parameterised statements and a strict column schema, the attacker can alter or delete other partners' orders, or read arbitrary tables, because the import runs with database write privileges.",
      "component": "CSV parser job -> orders database",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "A parser job imports each file into the orders database." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V1.3.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-89", "CWE-20"],
      "plainLanguage": "A partner could hide database commands inside a spreadsheet cell and change or read other people's orders.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Parse partner CSVs against a strict schema and use parameterised database writes",
        "given": "a partner CSV file is picked up by the parser job",
        "when": "rows are validated and written to the orders database",
        "then": "the parser enforces an explicit column schema, type and length checks per field, rejects the file on violation, and performs all writes through parameterised statements with a least-privilege database account"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Spoofing",
      "title": "Weak or shared SFTP credentials let an attacker impersonate a partner",
      "scenario": "The design names no authentication mechanism for the SFTP drop. If partners authenticate with shared or long-lived passwords rather than per-partner public keys, a leaked credential (or credential stuffing against the internet-facing SFTP port) lets an attacker upload order files as that partner and inject fraudulent orders into the business.",
      "component": "SFTP server partner authentication",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Partners upload CSV files of orders to our SFTP server." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V6.2.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-287", "CWE-798"],
      "plainLanguage": "If partners log in with a shared password, anyone who gets it can send us fake orders.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Per-partner key-based SFTP authentication",
        "given": "a partner connects to the SFTP server",
        "when": "the session authenticates",
        "then": "the server requires a per-partner account with a registered SSH public key, rejects password authentication, and the key can be revoked for a single partner without affecting others"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "ElevationOfPrivilege",
      "title": "One partner can read or overwrite another partner's order files",
      "scenario": "If all partners land in the same SFTP tree, or accounts are not chrooted/jailed to their own directory, a partner can list and download other partners' order files (customer and order data) or replace a competitor's file with modified rows before the parser runs. Path traversal in the uploaded filename could also place files outside the drop directory.",
      "component": "Partner file drop directory on SFTP server",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Partners upload CSV files of orders to our SFTP server." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V8.2.1", "V5.3.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-552", "CWE-22"],
      "plainLanguage": "Partners could end up seeing or changing each other's order files if they share one folder.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Isolate each partner to its own write-only drop location",
        "given": "an authenticated partner SFTP session",
        "when": "the partner lists, reads or writes files",
        "then": "the session is confined to that partner's own directory, cannot read or list any other partner's files, and server-side filenames are normalised so traversal sequences cannot escape the drop directory"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "DenialOfService",
      "title": "Multi-gigabyte or decompression-bomb uploads exhaust storage and the parser",
      "scenario": "The design accepts files of several gigabytes with no stated size or row limit. An attacker with partner access (or a buggy partner job) can upload many huge files, or a highly compressed archive that expands, filling SFTP storage and making the parser consume all memory or run for hours. Order imports for every other partner stall and the orders database may be left with half-imported files.",
      "component": "SFTP storage and CSV parser job",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Files can be up to several gigabytes." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V5.1.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-400", "CWE-770"],
      "plainLanguage": "Someone could upload huge files until the disk fills and imports for everyone stop.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Enforce size, count and resource limits on partner file drops",
        "given": "a partner uploads order files",
        "when": "the upload is stored or the parser processes it",
        "then": "a maximum file size, maximum row count, per-partner disk quota and per-partner concurrent/daily file limit are enforced, oversized files are rejected with an alert, and the parser streams records instead of loading the whole file into memory"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Tampering",
      "title": "Parser reads a file while it is still being written or after it is swapped",
      "scenario": "With gigabyte-sized uploads the parser can pick up a partially written file, or a partner can replace the file between the parser's validation step and its read. The result is truncated or substituted order data imported as if it were complete and approved, with no detection.",
      "component": "CSV parser job file pickup",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "A parser job imports each file into the orders database." },
        { "quote": "Files can be up to several gigabytes." }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-367"],
      "plainLanguage": "A giant file could be read halfway through uploading, so only part of the orders get imported.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Atomic hand-off and integrity check before import",
        "given": "a partner has finished uploading an order file",
        "when": "the parser job selects a file to process",
        "then": "only files moved to a completion marker/ready location are processed, the file is moved to an internal quarantine path the partner cannot write, its hash and expected record count are verified before any row is committed, and the import is applied as a single transaction or rolled back"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Repudiation",
      "title": "No way to prove which partner submitted a disputed order file",
      "scenario": "Partners dispute orders imported from their files, or fraudulent rows appear. Because the design records only that a parser job imported each file, there is no binding between the SFTP session identity, the exact file bytes and the resulting order rows, so the business cannot prove who submitted what and cannot scope a compromise to one partner.",
      "component": "SFTP ingest and import pipeline",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 3,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "A parser job imports each file into the orders database." }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-778"],
      "plainLanguage": "If a partner denies sending a bad order file, we have no proof of who uploaded it.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Bind imported orders to the uploading partner and file",
        "given": "a partner file is imported",
        "when": "order rows are written to the orders database",
        "then": "each row records the partner account, source filename, file hash and upload timestamp, and the ingest log of session identity, source address and file hash is retained in storage partners and the parser cannot modify"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Partner order data (customer PII) left readable on the SFTP server after import",
      "scenario": "Order CSVs contain customer and order details. If files stay in the drop area after import with broad filesystem or operator access and no retention limit, a compromise of the SFTP host or an over-privileged internal account yields a bulk archive of partner customer data across all partners and many months.",
      "component": "SFTP file storage",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Partners upload CSV files of orders to our SFTP server." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V14.1.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-212", "CWE-732"],
      "plainLanguage": "Old order files full of customer details could pile up on the server for anyone with access to grab.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Short retention and restricted access for uploaded order files",
        "given": "an order file has been successfully imported",
        "when": "the retention period for raw drops elapses",
        "then": "the file is deleted (or archived encrypted with access limited to a named role), storage is encrypted at rest, filesystem permissions deny all accounts except the SFTP and parser service identities, and deletions are logged"
      }
    }
  ]
}
